title: Negative information questions and answers review
focus: Build negative information questions, answer with nobody or nothing, and correct an assumption when the true answer is affirmative.
targetSkills: Negative information questions with singular olla forms
Negative information questions with plural olla forms

Negative information questions with plural action verbs

exercises.prompt: Write “Where aren't you?” in Finnish. Use Missä (“where”), ole (“be”), sinä (“you”). Address one person (sinä).
exercises.explanation: Singular refers to one person or one thing in these patterns. The inessive is the in-place form, answering where. In an ordinary negative information question, keep the question word first and use the negative verb: Miksi sinä et ole kotona? (“Why aren't you at home?”). Singular forms are minä en ole, sinä et ole and hän ei ole. Ole stays unchanged after the negative verb. The complete question means “Where aren't you”.
requiredSkills: Negative information questions with singular olla forms
exercises.targetSkill: Negative information questions with singular olla forms

exercises.prompt: Translate “Minä en ole kirjastossa.” into English.
acceptedAnswers: I am not in the library.
exercises.explanation: Singular refers to one person or one thing in these patterns. A pronoun stands in place of a name or noun. The answer supplies the requested information. A negative question does not require a negative answer: Miksi et ole kotona? can receive Koska olen koulussa (“Because I am at school”). When confirming an excluded place in a bounded comparison, En ole koulussa means I am not at school. Read the intended reply before choosing its form. The complete reply means “I am not in the library”.

exercises.prompt: Build “We are not in the library.” in Finnish.
exercises.explanation: Plural means more than one in this grammatical pattern. An addressed group replies with emme ole (“we are not”) when the reply is negative. An affirmative information answer still uses its ordinary affirmative verb: Olemme koulussa (“We are at school”). He refers to another group and keeps eivät ole in a negative reply about that group. The complete reply means “We are not in the library”.

exercises.prompt: Complete “What don't you eat?”: ____ sinä et syö? Write the full sentence. Use Mitä (“what”), sinä (“you”), syö (“eat”). Address one person (sinä).
exercises.explanation: Singular refers to one person or one thing in these patterns. The partitive is a word form used here for an amount, an action's object, or a substance or group description. Use the question word, the appropriate negative verb and the main verb's negative form: Miksi sinä et tule? (“Why aren't you coming?”). Form these negative main-verb forms by removing -n from the supplied I-form: tulen → tule, juon → juo, luen → lue. The negative form keeps the stem changes already present in the I-form. The complete question means “What don't you eat”.

exercises.prompt: Answer “Kuka lukee lehteä?”: write “Nobody is reading a newspaper.” in Finnish. Use lehteä (“a newspaper”), lue (“read”).
exercises.explanation: Singular refers to one person or one thing in these patterns. A stem is the part of a word to which an ending is attached. A weak stem uses the changed consonants shown in the construction steps; the strong stem keeps the corresponding strong consonants. Ei kukaan is a natural short reply to Kuka tulee? (“Who is coming?”). A full reply gives kukaan + ei + the negative main-verb form. Do not translate nobody by putting ei before an affirmative verb form, and do not use plural eivät with kukaan here. The complete reply means “Nobody is reading a newspaper”.

exercises.prompt: Correct the assumption: Answer “Miksi sinä et juo vettä?”: write “I am drinking water.” in Finnish. Use juoda (“to drink”), Minä (“I”), vettä (“water”).

exercises.prompt: Write “When aren't they coming?” in Finnish. Use he (“they”), Milloin (“when”), tule (“come”).
exercises.explanation: Plural means more than one in this grammatical pattern. With plural persons, the negative verb is emme, ette or eivät. The main verb's negative form does not take a plural personal ending: Miksi te ette tule? (“Why aren't you coming?” addressed to a group). The same negative stem serves every person. The complete question means “When aren't they coming”.
